finding: There is no live range for this job on the site today (live is null), so this is a first build, not a check. HELD: the luxury class still has no labor time printed with a unit. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2015 Corolla about $175-$241 (0.6 hr); midsize 2018 Chrysler Pacifica front-wheel drive about $121-$277 (0.7-1.0 hr); truck 2016 Tacoma 3.5L V6 about $190-$268 (0.7 hr); luxury not built. The three built totals bracket Jerry ($143-$223) and sit at or below RepairPal ($230-$335). RepairPal carries $144-$211 in labor, which is about 1.0-1.5 hours at this rate, against our 0.6-1.0 hours of warranty time; that difference is expected, since a warranty time is the low end of what a shop bills and a shop usually also charges a minimum and a relearn where the car needs one. A supportable first range for an easy-to-reach sensor on a mainstream vehicle is roughly $120-$335, taking our low and RepairPal's high. It should not be published as a single range: access varies enormously. Chrysler's own times for the same sensor on the same van are 0.7 hour with front-wheel drive and 2.9 hours with all-wheel drive, which adds about $265-$350 in labor, and YourMechanic's Lexus figures ($587-$882) show what a buried sensor costs. How solid the labor times are: the Tacoma time (0.7 hr, of which 0.1 is dealer paperwork) is Toyota's own figure for the example vehicle from its 2017 recall and is the best number here. The Pacifica times are Chrysler's, for the example vehicle, but read from a trade-press summary of the bulletin; the bulletin itself was not found on NHTSA. The Corolla time is borrowed from a 2006 Toyota campaign on the 2001-2002 Echo and Prius, a different engine, so it is weak; a 2003 Nissan campaign that fits a whole sensor kit (crankshaft plus camshaft sensors) on a Sentra in 0.5 hrs. agrees with it in scale but is a cross-check only. None of the three says a crankshaft relearn is included; Hyundai lists the scan-tool step as a separate 0.3 on the Genesis and GM requires a relearn on the Volt, so where a car needs one, expect it to be added. Parts: an aftermarket sensor stated as new was found only for the Pacifica ($36.75); the Corolla, Tacoma and Genesis low ends are genuine sensors at an online discount, and no aftermarket sensor for the Tacoma 3.5L V6 was found at all, so their low ends are higher than a shop using an aftermarket sensor might quote. The luxury parts are now loaded: the genuine Hyundai sensor for the 2015 Genesis lists at $128.37 and sells for $91.37 online. What is missing and why: (1) luxury hours: the only maker figure found, Hyundai's 0.3 for the Genesis 3.8L (plus a separate 0.3 scan-tool step), is printed with no unit and was read from a third-party copy; another Hyundai bulletin for the same car on NHTSA prints its times the same way, with no unit, so it stays a cross-check only. If it is hours, the Genesis would build to roughly $127-$176 for the sensor alone and $163-$224 with the relearn step, but that is not published here. On this pass, bulletins from GM (Cadillac XT5), Lexus (RX350), Infiniti, Honda, Jaguar Land Rover and Ford/Lincoln were loaded and none prints a crankshaft position sensor replacement time with a unit: they print no time, refer to a published labor guide, or cover a different part (the sensor rotor, a reprogramming, a timing chain); (2) each built class rests on a single stated time, so every range is narrow and understates what shops bill; (3) no full-size pickup time was found, so the truck class is a midsize pickup. To finish: find a luxury maker time printed with a unit, load the Chrysler bulletin itself, and load aftermarket prices (Denso, NTK, Standard) from pages that state the part is new. An estimate is never a quote and never a diagnosis.
extras: A quote often adds a diagnosis fee, because the same stall, no-start or check-engine codes can come from wiring, the connector, the toothed wheel the sensor reads, or the camshaft sensor. It may also add a crankshaft position relearn with a scan tool, a new O-ring or seal, shop supplies and sales tax. Where the sensor sits behind the starter, under the intake or above a driveshaft or transfer case, removing and refitting those parts adds labor (Chrysler allows 2.9 hours on an all-wheel-drive Pacifica against 0.7 with front-wheel drive). A sensor that has seized in its bore and breaks on removal adds time. Shops often suggest replacing the camshaft sensor at the same visit; that is a separate job.
